summary.text: 儿 is the simplified form of 兒. The older graph depicts a young child, though the identity of its upper feature is disputed.

formation.text: The traditional graph 兒 is pictographic: a person-like lower form and an upper feature together depict a child. The upper feature is interpreted either as an infant’s unclosed fontanel or as paired hair buns. Modern 儿 is a reduced form of 兒.

components.text: In 兒, the lower person-like element contributes to the picture of a child; it is not a sound component.
The upper part of 兒 is described as 臼-like. One interpretation identifies it as an infant’s unclosed fontanel; another sees paired hair buns, so its depicted feature remains disputed.

history.text: 兒 is recorded in oracle-bone, bronze, manuscript, and seal-script forms. Historical explanations identify it as a child graph, though they differ over whether its upper feature depicts an unclosed fontanel or paired hair buns.

Modern 儿 reduces 兒 by omitting its upper 臼-like portion. The same shape also has an independent standing-person use as a form of 人; that separate use does not explain the simplified child graph. The exact adoption date is unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The upper feature in the early child graph is interpreted either as an unclosed fontanel or as paired hair buns; its precise depiction remains unresolved.
The relative dates and semantic links among the recorded child, son, address, young-person, and suffix uses are not established by the cited examples and glosses.
No internal sound component is proposed for 兒. The reported readings and reconstructions concern the word represented by the whole character, not a component within the graph.

senses.text: A historical dictionary glosses 兒 as a young child, and the graph is recorded in early inscriptional corpora. The semantic context of the earliest graph examples and the first occurrence of the spoken word are not securely dated.
Son is a recorded sense, but its emergence relative to the child sense is not dated.

senses.gloss: address to a child or younger person; parental address or self-reference
senses.period: Han-attributed text and later examples; exact chronology unresolved
senses.text: 呼兒 in a Han-attributed poem addresses a child or household dependent. Later examples include parental address and self-reference, but the poem’s disputed attribution and later transmission do not establish a contemporary Han witness or a sequence of semantic development.
A young-person sense appears in later cited material, but its first date and connection to the child sense are unresolved.
Suffix use is recorded, but its emergence and any semantic path from the child sense are not established.

senses.period: modern simplified writing; exact adoption date unresolved
senses.text: Simplified 儿 writes the child graph 兒 in reduced form. This graphic change does not show that its child meaning developed from the separate person-shaped use of 儿.

limitations.text: The evidence records several senses but does not establish their full chronology or semantic connections, so no developmental links are asserted.
The earliest attestation of the spoken child word is not securely dated here; the poem’s date is an attribution, and its surviving transmission is later.

overview.text: 儿 is the simplified form of 兒, whose older graph depicts a young child. Its upper feature may be an unclosed soft spot or paired hair buns; the interpretation is disputed.

components.text: This person-like part contributes to the historical picture of a child.
The upper part may depict an unclosed soft spot or paired hair buns; its meaning is disputed.

takeaway.text: The child meaning belongs to the whole graph 兒; simplified 儿 is its reduced writing, distinct from the separate person-shaped use of 儿.

relationships.text: In 兒, the lower person-like element contributes to the proposed child depiction.
The upper 臼-like part has competing interpretations as an infant’s head feature or paired hair buns.
Modern 儿 reduces 兒 by omitting the upper 臼-like portion.
